## Overview

This project packages **four modern fine-tuning techniques** into **two runnable local pipelines** on a consumer NVIDIA GPU. You download a base language model, train small **adapter layers** on your machine, then chat with the result in **two Gradio web UIs** — no cloud API required.

| Project | Model | Method | Best for | Web UI |
|---------|-------|--------|----------|--------|
| **1 — Instruction Tune** | Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct | **QLoRA + SFT** | Domain format, instructions, Q&A style | port **7861** |
| **2 — Preference Align** | Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct | **ORPO + DoRA** | Tone, style, chosen vs rejected answers | port **7860** |

**GitHub:** [sophalchan/modern-llm-finetuning-lab](https://github.com/sophalchan/modern-llm-finetuning-lab)

**Stack:** PyTorch · PEFT · TRL · bitsandbytes · Gradio · Hugging Face

::: {.callout-note}
**Results & testing:** Training benchmarks, sample outputs, loss curves, and GPU metrics will be published in a **separate follow-up article**. This page covers background, motivation, architecture, structure, and how to run the lab.
:::

## What it does (plain English)

A base chat model like **Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct** already knows general language. This lab **teaches it new behaviour** in two different ways:

- **Project 1 (QLoRA):** show instruction → answer examples; the model learns to follow that format and style (**supervised fine-tuning**).
- **Project 2 (ORPO + DoRA):** show good vs bad answer pairs; the model learns to **prefer** better responses (**preference alignment**).

Both projects load the base model in **4-bit** so training and inference fit an **8 GB GPU**. After training you get a small adapter folder (~40 MB) — a custom layer on top of the base model — and chat in the browser without terminal commands.

## Background of the Study

### The problem: full fine-tuning does not fit on a laptop

Large language models (LLMs) with 7B–70B parameters contain billions of floating-point weights. **Full fine-tuning** updates every weight during training. That requires:

- Tens of gigabytes of VRAM just to hold the model in memory
- Additional memory for optimizer states (Adam stores momentum per parameter)
- More memory still for activations during the backward pass

On a typical laptop GPU (8–12 GB), full fine-tuning of even a 7B model is **impossible** without multi-GPU clusters or cloud instances costing dollars per hour.

### The industry response: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)

Research and open-source tools converged on a practical compromise: **freeze the base model** and train only a tiny set of **adapter parameters**.

| Era | Technique | Key idea |
|-----|-----------|----------|
| 2019–2021 | **LoRA** | Add low-rank matrices (A × B) to attention layers; train ~0.1–1% of params |
| 2023 | **QLoRA** | Store frozen base in 4-bit; train LoRA adapters in higher precision → 8B on 16 GB |
| 2023–2024 | **Unsloth** | Optimized CUDA kernels for faster LoRA training on consumer GPUs |
| 2024 | **ORPO** | Combine SFT + preference alignment in **one** training step (no separate DPO) |
| 2024 | **DoRA** | Decompose weight updates into direction + magnitude → closer to full fine-tune quality |

### Why these four techniques together

Each technique solves a different bottleneck:

1. **QLoRA** — makes the model **fit in memory**
2. **Unsloth** — makes training **fast enough to iterate** (Project 1 Llama path, 16 GB+)
3. **ORPO** — makes **preference alignment simple** (no two-stage SFT → DPO pipeline)
4. **DoRA** — makes **adapters more expressive** without full-parameter cost

### Academic and professional context

Fine-tuning sits between **prompt engineering** (zero training, limited control) and **training from scratch** (prohibitively expensive). For portfolio and production work — custom chatbots, domain Q&A, internal copilots, RAG answer formatting — **adapter-based fine-tuning** is the standard middle path used by Hugging Face, TRL, PEFT, and most ML engineering teams.

This lab implements that path **locally and transparently**: YAML configs, readable Python scripts, shared inference engine, and browser UIs — so every stage (load, train, save, generate) can be inspected and explained in an interview or capstone defense.

### The 8 GB constraint

Many students and professionals have **8 GB laptop GPUs** (e.g. RTX 3060 Laptop, RTX 2000 Ada). Standard 7B/8B recipes assume 16–24 GB. This project adds **`project1_low_vram.yaml`** and **`project2_low_vram.yaml`** using **Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct** — a capable instruct model that fits 8 GB with 4-bit loading, gradient checkpointing, and batch size 1.

## Motivation of the Study

### Personal and professional motivation

- **Run locally, own your data** — no API keys, no per-token billing, sensitive prompts stay on your machine
- **Portfolio depth** — recruiters can clone, train, and chat in under an hour; architecture is inspectable
- **Bridge teaching and engineering** — same stack used in AI/ML courses (LoRA, SFT, alignment) and in industry (PEFT, TRL, Hugging Face)
- **Honest hardware documentation** — clearly state what works on 8 GB vs what needs 16 GB+
- **Two real use cases in one repo** — instruction tuning (Project 1) vs preference alignment (Project 2), not just one demo script

### Technical motivation

| Goal | How this project addresses it |
|------|-------------------------------|
| Reproducible experiments | YAML configs separate hyperparameters from code |
| Fair comparison | Same base model (Qwen 1.5B), same 4-bit stack, different trainers |
| Fast demo iteration | `max_steps: 10` proves pipeline in seconds; scale up for production |
| Shared inference | One `inference_engine.py` serves CLI + both UIs |
| Dual Web UIs | Gradio on ports 7860 and 7861 for live demos |
| No gated models on 8 GB path | Qwen 1.5B is public — no HF token required for low-VRAM configs |

### Research questions this lab explores

1. Can **QLoRA instruction tuning** run end-to-end on an 8 GB consumer GPU?
2. Can **ORPO + DoRA preference alignment** run on the same hardware with the same base model?
3. How do **SFT (Project 1)** and **ORPO (Project 2)** differ in architecture when sharing inference code?
4. What is the **memory and time cost** of training vs inference on laptop-class GPUs?

(Answers with metrics and sample outputs — in the upcoming results article.)

## The 4 techniques (simple definitions)

| Technique | What it does |
|-----------|----------------|
| **QLoRA** | Keeps the base model in 4-bit; trains only tiny LoRA adapter layers → fits on one GPU |
| **Unsloth** | Optimized training kernels → 2–5× faster (optional Llama 8B path, 16 GB+) |
| **ORPO** | Aligns preferences in **one step** — no separate SFT then DPO |
| **DoRA** | Weight-decomposed LoRA — updates direction and magnitude separately for better quality |

## Project 1 — QLoRA instruction tuning (deep dive)

### Architectural goal

Project 1 teaches the model **instruction-following format**: user asks a question → assistant gives a helpful answer. Training uses **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)** with **QLoRA** — the base model stays frozen in 4-bit; only LoRA adapters receive gradients.

### Design pattern: separation of concerns

```text
┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐   ┌─────────────┐
│   CONFIG    │   │   TRAINING  │   │  INFERENCE  │   │     UI      │
│  YAML recipe│ → │  SFTTrainer │ → │ PEFT engine │ → │ Gradio 7861 │
└─────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘   └─────────────┘
```

### Project 1 architecture — training

::: {.architecture-diagram}
```{mermaid}
%%{init: {
  "theme": "base",
  "themeVariables": { "fontSize": "14px" },
  "flowchart": { "curve": "linear", "padding": 14, "nodeSpacing": 24, "rankSpacing": 34 }
}}%%
flowchart TB
    C["project1_low_vram.yaml"]
    T["train_qwen_qlora.py"]
    D["yahma/alpaca-cleaned<br/>instruction + output"]
    M["Qwen2.5-1.5B · 4-bit frozen"]
    L["LoRA adapters · r=8 · trainable"]
    S["TRL SFTTrainer"]
    O[("lora_model_qwen/")]

    C --> T
    D --> T
    T --> M
    T --> L
    M --> S
    L --> S
    S --> O

    style C fill:#d6eaf8,stroke:#2471a3
    style O fill:#d5f5e3,stroke:#1e8449
```
:::

**Training stages (step by step):**

1. **Load config** — model ID, dataset, LoRA rank, max steps
2. **Load base model in 4-bit** (bitsandbytes NF4) — ~4× less VRAM than FP16
3. **Attach LoRA** to attention + MLP layers (`q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj`, `o_proj`, `gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`)
4. **Enable gradient checkpointing** — trades compute for memory (critical on 8 GB)
5. **Format dataset** as chat messages → apply Qwen chat template
6. **SFTTrainer** — loss on assistant tokens only; batch size 1 + gradient accumulation 4
7. **Save adapters** to `lora_model_qwen/` (~40 MB; base model stays on Hugging Face cache)

**LoRA in one equation:** effective weight = frozen W + (A × B), where A and B are small matrices with rank r=8.

**When you click Send:**

1. Gradio calls `chat()` → `get_engine("lora_model_qwen")`
2. Engine loads once (singleton cache) — base Qwen 1.5B in 4-bit + LoRA adapters
3. Question wrapped in Qwen chat template → tokenized → `model.generate()`
4. Assistant portion decoded and shown in chat window

**Status line example:**

> **Ready — Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (QLoRA)**

### Project 1 config (`project1_low_vram.yaml`)

| Setting | Value | Why |
|---------|-------|-----|
| `model_id` | Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct | Public model; fits 8 GB |
| `dataset_name` | yahma/alpaca-cleaned | General instruction → answer pairs |
| `train_samples` | 200 | Enough for demo; scale up for production |
| `max_seq_length` | 512 | Limits VRAM per example |
| `lora_r` | 8 | Small adapters; low memory |
| `max_steps` | 10 | Fast pipeline proof (~10–30 s) |
| `output_dir` | lora_model_qwen | Saved adapters |

### Memory design (8 GB GPU)

| Component | Approx. VRAM |
|-----------|--------------|
| Qwen 1.5B in 4-bit | ~1–1.5 GB |
| LoRA adapters + optimizer (training) | ~1–2 GB |
| Activations + grad checkpointing | ~2–4 GB |
| **Training total** | ~5–7 GB ✓ |
| **Inference total** | ~2–3 GB ✓ |

## Project 2 — ORPO + DoRA preference alignment

### Architectural goal

Project 2 teaches the model **which answers are better** using chosen vs rejected pairs in a **single ORPO training step** with **DoRA** adapters (direction + magnitude decomposition).

### Project 1 vs Project 2

| | **Project 1 — QLoRA + SFT** | **Project 2 — ORPO + DoRA** |
|---|---------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Goal** | Instruction format & content | Prefer good over bad answers |
| **Trainer** | `SFTTrainer` | `ORPOTrainer` |
| **Data** | instruction + output | question + chosen + rejected |
| **Adapters** | Standard LoRA | DoRA |
| **Output** | `lora_model_qwen/` | `orpo_qwen_final/` |
| **UI** | http://localhost:7861 | http://localhost:7860 |

Both share `inference_engine.py` and the same 4-bit loading path.

## Step-by-step — run locally

### Step 1 — Clone and install

```bash
git clone https://github.com/sophalchan/modern-llm-finetuning-lab.git
cd modern-llm-finetuning-lab
bash scripts/install.sh
source .venv/bin/activate
python scripts/check_environment.py
```

Requires **Linux**, **NVIDIA GPU**, **Python 3.11**, and CUDA PyTorch.

### Step 2 — Train Project 1 (QLoRA, 8 GB)

```bash
python project1_unsloth_qlora/train_qwen_qlora.py --config project1_low_vram.yaml
```

Creates `lora_model_qwen/`.

### Step 3 — Train Project 2 (ORPO + DoRA, 8 GB)

```bash
python project2_orpo_dora/train_qwen_orpo.py --config project2_low_vram.yaml
```

Creates `orpo_qwen_final/`.

### Step 4 — Launch both Web UIs

```bash
pip install gradio
python app_ui_project1.py   # Project 1 → http://localhost:7861
python app_ui.py            # Project 2 → http://localhost:7860
```

Or use shortcuts:

```bash
bash scripts/run_ui_project1.sh
bash scripts/run_ui.sh
```

### Step 5 — Terminal inference (optional)

```bash
python project1_unsloth_qlora/infer_qwen_qlora.py --prompt "Explain QLoRA in plain language."
python project2_orpo_dora/infer_qwen_orpo.py --prompt "What is ORPO fine-tuning?"
```

### Step 6 — Llama 8B + Unsloth (optional, 16 GB+ VRAM)

```bash
pip install "unsloth[colab-new] @ git+https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth.git"
# Set HF_TOKEN in .env for gated Llama weights
python project1_unsloth_qlora/train_llama31_unsloth.py
```

## Software design patterns used

| Pattern | Where | Why |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Configuration as code | YAML configs | Reproducible experiments without code changes |
| Separation of concerns | train / infer / UI / engine | Each module has one responsibility |
| Singleton cache | `get_engine()` | Avoid reloading GPU model every message |
| Fail fast | `require_cuda()` | Clear error if no GPU |
| Adapter pattern (ML) | PEFT LoRA / DoRA | Small trainable patch on frozen base |
| Thin client UI | Gradio → engine only | UI can change without touching ML code |
| Shared inference layer | Both projects | DRY — one loader for all paths |

## Advantages of this project

| Advantage | Why it matters |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Runs locally** | No API cost; data stays on your machine |
| **8 GB GPU works** | Both projects use Qwen 1.5B + 4-bit + low-VRAM configs |
| **Two training paradigms** | SFT vs ORPO in one repo — fair comparison |
| **Dual Web UIs** | Live demo for portfolio and interviews |
| **Shared inference engine** | Same code path for CLI and browser |
| **YAML-driven** | Change model, steps, LR without editing Python |
| **Public base model** | No HF token required for 8 GB path |
| **Transparent architecture** | Every stage inspectable for learning and defense |

## Hardware note

| Requirement | Detail |
|-------------|--------|
| GPU | NVIDIA — **8 GB** works (Qwen 1.5B low-VRAM configs); **16 GB+** for Llama 8B / Qwen 7B |
| OS | Linux + CUDA |
| Python | **3.11** recommended (3.14 breaks some ML packages) |
| Disk | ~20 GB+ for Hugging Face model cache |

Verified on **NVIDIA RTX 2000 Ada Laptop GPU (7.6 GB VRAM)**.

## Limitations

- Demo configs use **10 training steps** — pipeline proof only; production needs thousands of steps and more data
- **Unsloth + Llama 8B** path needs 16 GB+ VRAM and may have package conflicts on some setups
- Web UIs run **locally** — not hosted on GitHub Pages (requires your GPU)
- Training datasets are public Hugging Face samples — swap in your own data for domain-specific models
- Results and benchmarks documented in a **separate upcoming article**
